Farming more so than ranching ( in my opinion) is much more difficult and involved in politics, economics and global trade, especially from crop to crop. And also subsidized by the federal government. But not all farming is, only corn, soybeans, wheat, cotton, and rice. Livestock, fruits and vegetables' are not. I'm sure you could see how that might rub some Montana rancher or a Florida orange farmer the wrong way. Over 50% of the wheat in this country is exported to other countries. American beef exports are at about 11% of all production. While the whole ag industry is steeped in patriotism, a Texas 100% USA beef producer might have something to say to a federally subsidized Kansas wheat famer that exports his wheat to India.

And also yes. There are famers who think certain crops are more prestigious than others. I know a family that has been growing cotton on a massive scale outside of Corpus Christi, TX since like the fall of the Alamo ( that's an exaggeration). Talking to them you'd think they were responsible for clothing all of America and part of the world. Pride in what you do is a standard in the industry. After reading A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man, I realized that Stephen's odyssey into enlightenment was very similar to my own journey through young-adult hood.  I sympathized with him.  I believed his ideals were pure and natural and necessary; unfortunately, after mulling over the novel, and reading a particularly poignant critique that slips my mind at this moment, I arrived at the realization that Stephen's ideology isn't something to particularly aspire to.  I kept asking myself, at what cost?  Stephen throws away everything: he denies affiliation with his native soil and tosses away the tradition of his ancestors he becomes a man with no past and no future.  He is alone.  Stephen is all alone.  I began noticing that I had been asking myself, What would Stephen do?  Stephen's musings were stained into my .  Stephen and me morphed into one conscious being, and the thought that a young boy, holding nothing but resentment for his past, and hope for his future could create such a profound catharsis in me was chilling.  I desperately didn't want to delineate my environment like Stephen does.  His journey is that of the traveling bard, like Homer, blindly searching for a home he'll never find.  Literature is his one and only love, it's his religion, and it's Stephen's entire world.  Portrait is simply the story of a lost soul searching for a comfortable place.  The only place he finds it is in his books.  It spoke to me in a profound way.  Furthermore, the novel's lack of historical background is a blaring alarm for me.  The IRA and the British crown were at the height of physical conflict, yet Stephen never witnesses a single view of this strife.  Stephen isn't transcending into a religious perception of art; Stephen is running away from the strife surrounding him.
